An insufferable but well-meaning feel-good drama.
It's an inspirational true story about a child with special needs and how he transforms his dad for the better.

You already know exactly what “The Unbreakable Boy” will be when you sit down to watch it, and it doesn’t disappoint. This is ersatz sentimental Americana at its most shamelessly emotionally manipulative
The Unbreakable Boy takes a turn toward something more sentimental than tough. Faith-based movies would be better if their happy endings weren’t always so rosy.
'The Unbreakable Boy' will satisfy the terminally vanilla moviegoers, but the rest will see right through its game.
the real struggle here is trying to connect with this film beyond a wan appreciation that a father finally learned how to love his son for who he is. Good for him, I guess?

Watching The Unbreakable Boy, one should not wonder if we are referencing a teenage boy on the autism spectrum, stricken with brittle bone disease, or the selfish, narcissistic, father who overcomes his dependency through a belief in God. Yet here we are.

The film should have been about Austin’s struggles and triumphs, but it shifts the focus to Zachary Levi's alcoholic father. The drama tries too hard to tug at your emotions while losing focus on its ambitions. The performances are good.

The character is largely sanded down to a toothy smile and a nagging sense that his dad always feels “close and far away at the same time, like even though I’m right there he doesn’t really see me.” He might as well be describing the film itself.
This solid faith-based chronicle of a family navigating both disability and alcohol abuse has several things working in its favor.

There's plenty of melodrama about medical conditions and financial struggles, but there's an over-use of movie clichés that sugarcoat the truth...by presenting a perky boy with autism as if he's some kind of good luck charm used for the family's benefit.
The decision to lean more toward Scott’s story that Austin’s doesn’t break the film, but it just leaves a feeling that there could have been a far more emotional impact.
The movie is a very sincere and good-hearted adaptation, but it loses focus by trying to include too many elements of the real-life story.

quote: I suppose your reaction to it all comes down to your willingness to vicariously walk a mile in the LeRettes’ shoes, a journey Gunn honors and stays true to.
All the pieces are here for a heartwarming classic of a film, yet the script could not quite flesh out a story impactful nor focused enough to justify our journey with these characters.
While I’m never opposed to a good message, the execution here, under director Jon Gunn’s guidance, often feels a bit stifled.
The Unbreakable Boy could have benefited from a stronger infusion of Austin’s vitality.
The Unbreakable Boy works hard, very hard, to pull your heartstrings... But at a certain point it stops feeling inspirational and more like misery porn.
Although based on actual events, the film is executed in a saccharine, clichéd manner that leaves you feeling more annoyed than uplifted.
A sweet, inspiring portrait of a family and a marriage that was a lot better than I expected it to be.

This movie didn’t tell the story I expected. ... I thought we would see his optimism and joy confront the world’s cruelty and cynicism. ... This story is about Scott, while Austin serves as the catalyst for his father’s transformation.

Zachary Levi works well enough as the lead, but it's a role beset with odd lines and unmoored choices. It's a film that largely rests on an edifice of clichés, contrivances, and ungrounded choices, needing greater development to actually land.
The type of joyous and inspiring story of positivity over adversity that the world really could use right now.

With Gunn, happy endings materialize out of thin air. Forced? I would say so. But then I’m a cynic. I’m also on the spectrum. And I feel justified in stating me and my brethren deserve a much more honorable depiction than this misguided treacle.
The Unbreakable Boy is yet another winner from Jon Gunn, easily one of the most authentic and gifted faith-based and faith-inspired filmmakers working today.
Undeniably sentimental and sappy, this true story of a flawed dad who struggles to bond with his special needs son will nonetheless melt even the coldest of hearts.

“The Unbreakable Boy” eventually wants little to do with Austin, becoming a tale of a father’s redemption, which gives the effort the faint scent of narcissism, losing sight of its most intriguing personality.
